description.contents: Analysis of Functions of One VariableThis course introduces various functions, including polynomials, rational functions, power functions, exponential, and logarithmic functions. Key properties such as domain, range, increasing and decreasing, convex and concave, asymptotes, and invertibility are examined in detail.Solving Equations, Inequalities and LimitsStudents learn to solve different types of equations, inequalities, and limits. The course covers a range of techniques to solve these problems.Differentiation Techniques and ApplicationStudents learn to calculate derivatives of functions of one or more variables and apply them to tangent lines, tangent planes, elasticities, higher-order derivatives, implicit differentiation, and linear and quadratic approximations.Integration Techniques and ApplicationsThe course introduces different integrals and integration techniques, such as definite, indefinite, and improper integrals, integration by substitution, and their applications in calculating consumer and producer surplus.Comparative Statics and Financial Economics.Students will learn about the degree of homogeneity, Euler's theorem, and finite and infinite geometric series that can be used to compute present and future values.OptimizationSeveral techniques and concepts for unconstrained and constrained optimisation are introduced, including the Lagrange method and the interpretation of the Lagrange multiplier.
description.objectives: The aim of this course is to let students obtain a solid understanding of the mathematics required in economics and necessary to obtain a bachelor's degree in Economics and Business Economics.After completing this course, students should be able to:demonstrate an understanding of mathematical methods commonly used in economics and apply them accurately to solve relevant problems;utilize correct mathematical notation and apply applicable definitions and theorems to reason mathematically with clarity and accuracy;identify mathematical techniques needed to solve economic problems and correctly interpret the conclusions.

description.contents: This course focuses on the main theoretical concepts in economics and business administration - some of their intellectual history and meaning - as well as their importance for understanding real phenomena in society. The aim is to understand how individuals and organisations operate within the context of society and its goals, laws and regulations, which aim to constrain or encourage certain behaviours. Subjects include incentives and decision-making, the firm as an entity, markets as competitive arenas, entrepreneurship and business strategies, the role of government, wealth, money, and public goods. Students obtain insight and comprehensive knowledge of themes that are central to economics and business. To this end, current subjects in the media will serve as illustrations and content for practical assignments (that will be offered in class). Examples are taken from business cases and regulatory matters. Lastly, students will be given sneak previews of how these subjects will be relevant later in the bachelor programme, including guest lectures by professors who teach bachelor courses further down the program.A foundation will be laid for students to independently begin carrying out academic thinking and relate their findings to the existing academic literature. In the tutorials, students will learn how to apply the week's literature to a modern-day subject, ranging from dynamic online pricing, and the power of Big Tech, to the green transition. This includes learning how to read and evaluate academic literature based on critical economic and/or business thinking.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course:the student will be able to explain how individuals and organisations operate within the context of society;the student will be able to relate and compare different theories of economic thinking as an intellectual history;the student will be able to apply economic and business administration theories to real phenomena and current practical problems;the student will be able to evaluate relevant economics and business administration literature;the student is able to use AI in a responsible manner.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Business Administration, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: This subject is divided into two parts: In periods 1 and 2, Principles of Economics and Business Administration consists solely of study skills and is called Skills and Connect. In period 3, it will focus on economic theories about digital businesses, sustainability, ethics, fiscal economics, and academic skills.During the Skills and Connect tutorials, students learn how to formulate goals, get acquainted with the university, practice various study methods, time management, and learn to reflect on their progress, enabling them to achieve their set goals. During the Skills and Connect classes, various social events are also organised to connect with their class and the university as a whole.The second part focuses on gaining an overview of theories related to ethics, taxation, sustainability, and digital platforms. During the lectures in period 3, the lecturers explain the relevant theory that plays a role in these areas. The tutorials discuss the literature that students need to prepare for that week. The goal is for students to apply the theory to a platform of their choice in which they merge insights from the digital platform, taxation, ethics and sustainability.
description.objectives: After successful completion of this course, the following learning objectives have been achieved:students are able to formulate their study goals and reflect on them. They will have gained more independence regarding the study behaviour required at university;students have obtained an overview and knowledge of digital platforms, taxation, ethics and sustainabilty. They understand how the digital platform can be approach from a business, taxation, sustainable, ethical perspective;students are able to write an academic text in which they use the academic literature discussed during the tutorial to answer a research question, combining insights from the four topics addressed during the course;students understand the main concepts explained in the articles and can relate them to the concepts explained during the lecture;students are able to write an academic text;students know how to use and integrate the academic sources in a coherent manner in their text;students are able to use AI in a responsible manner for the assignment;students are able to employ an academic writing style;student are able to apply APA standards in their assignment.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Business Administration, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: Accounting is fundamental to the functioning of organisations and economies. In this course, students will learn to identify and record the economic transactions of an organisation and to communicate the economic results of an organisation to outsiders such as investors, banks, and government agencies using financial statements.We will begin by analysing the basic structure of organisations and the information needs of owners and other stakeholders. Next, we will discuss how accounting systems are used to fulfil these needs and how accrual accounting is different from the recording of cash flows. We place much emphasis on learning the techniques to adequately record and value basic economic transactions, discussing different types of assets (including cash, inventories, accounts receivable, plant and equipment, intangible assets, and financial assets) and liabilities (including accounts payable, notes payable, and bonds). We will also discuss different types of transactions with shareholders, including issuing shares and paying dividends. Finally, students will learn to read financial statements and make decisions based on information contained in financial statements. Throughout the course, we pay attention to the fundamental values associated with the accounting profession - such as independence and objectivity - and to the important different roles of accountants in organisations and societies.
description.objectives: After successful completion of this course, students will:understand the fundamentals of bookkeeping and financial accounting, including the accounting equation and the difference between accrual accounting and cash accounting;understand the transaction recording process and the accounting cycle, and be able to journalise common economic transactions;be able to categorise, record and value different types of assets and liabilities;understand the basics of the structure of corporations, including the distinction between ownership and management;understand the main financial statements (balance sheet, income statement, and statement of cash flows) and be able to perform basic financial statement analyses.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: Economics is the scientific analysis of questions associated with allocating and distributing scarce resources. Microeconomics investigates these questions at the fundamental level of individual economic agents such as consumers, firms and other micro-level organisations. In addition, we look at the consequences of individual decisions for aggregate (market) outcomes. The course, therefore, mainly deals with individual consumption choices and firms' production decisions. By aggregating these choices to demand and supply curves, the course introduces the notion of an equilibrium in a market economy. An important aspect is the analysis of the properties of such an equilibrium with respect to allocative efficiency. Furthermore, instances in which the market mechanism fails are introduced. The discussion of these market failures revolves around market imperfections (like monopolies), the provision of public goods (like defence and security) and externalities (like pollution). Last but not least, the analytical tool called game theory - which allows the analysis of strategic conflict situations - is presented and applied to economic problems. Given the feedback from the past course evaluations, we will expand the material shown in the main lectures.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will:have knowledge about the key concepts of microeconomics like optimisation, equilibrium, efficiency and welfare losses;understand the role of optimisation in microeconomic behaviour;be able to model and analyse how consumers optimise utility;be able to model and analyse how producers optimise profits in different markets (competitive markets, duopolies and monopolies);understand how market failures can arise, and be able to calculate the associated welfare losses and know how to prevent or repair market failures;be able to apply these theories and models by analysing and solving simple problems.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: The course covers:elementary macroeconomic facts, concepts and frameworks such as national accounting, the role of banks and central banks within the monetary system and the economy in general, the quantity theory, structural and frictional unemployment, deflators and Okun's Law;static general equilibrium models for a closed as well as an open economy;neoclassical business cycle theory, including the IS-LM model, the Mundell-Fleming model, the AD-AS model and the Phillips-curve;the Lucas-critique regarding the prediction of the effects of macroeconomic policymaking;a brief overview of the history and development of macroeconomics and the positioning of the course material in the broader historical perspective of macroeconomic thinking and its historical development;illustrations and applications based on recent macroeconomic developments.The course material studied in the course Macroeconomics 1 provides students with the required theoretical and conceptual background that will allow them to successfully participate in the subsequent courses Money and Banking, International Money and Finance and Macroeconomics 2. Moreover, the course Macroeconomics 1 introduces a number of topics that will be developed further in the aforementioned second-year courses.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students:can define and explain the most important macroeconomic concepts, discuss some important macroeconomic developments since World War II, and describe the most widely used theoretical models;can apply these models and theoretical insights in order to demonstrate how the economy reacts to macroeconomic shocks, such as changes in government purchases, taxes and the money supply;can identify, interpret and analyse recent macroeconomic events.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: This course reviews and explains the basic statistical concepts and techniques in Economics and Business Economics. It will also discuss how to identify and solve potential problems in data and results.The topics addressed in this course are divided into three groups:Basic descriptive techniques:the hierarchy of data types: measures of central location, dispersion, skewness, and graphical techniques;quantifying the relationship between two quantitative variables: correlation, covariance and the linear regression equation.Basic probability rules and distributions:probability calculus: probability rules, marginal and conditional probabilities and joint probability tables;discrete probability distributions: expectation and variance and specifically the Binomial and Poisson distributions, including the application of tables;continuous probability distributions: Uniform and (standard) Normal distributions, including the application of tables;bivariate distributions (covariance and correlation) and linear combinations of random variables: expectation and variance;random sampling, independent and identically distributed variables and sample distributions of the mean and proportion.Inferential statistics:theory of estimation: estimators (unbiased, efficient, and consistent), confidence intervals for the population mean and population proportion, including T-distribution;theory of testing: testing hypotheses on mean and proportion, the p-value, the power of a test, and finding the probability of a type two error;finding the desired sample size;application of the sign test for the median of ordinal scaled variables or for quantitative scaled variables.This list of topics will be extended in year 2 by the subsequent course Statistics 2 for Economics.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: understand the concept of probability and apply the basic rules for probability calculations;understand and use basic discrete and continuous random variables and their parameters;understand and apply the distribution of a sample mean and connected t-statistic;describe the quality of estimators, the concept of statistical hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals;list the basic statistical techniques in the field of exploratory data analysis of one or two variables and inferential statistics of one or two variables;comprehend the procedure underlying each of these techniques;describe the purpose of each technique and the conditions for its validity and recognise the circumstances in which each technique can be used;interpret and report the results of these techniques correctly;critically assess the findings in academic publications and research reports that are based on these techniques.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: Skills and ConnectThe Skills and Connect tutorials in period 4 will focus on two topics: Excel and presentation skills. After successful completion, students will be able to use the acquired skills independently for both personal, business and study purposes. They know how to set up a dataset, work with several formulas and create (pivot) tables and graphs. The presentation skills tutorials will teach students to use rhetoric and non-verbal communication to improve their pitch. They will learn how to give feedback to others and will be able to write a good pitch. Research SkillsDuring periods 5 and 6 of the course, students will learn how to conduct research. In period 5, we will cover the basics of empirical research methodology. At an introductory level, students will learn the most commonly used empirical designs: experiments, regression control, regression discontinuity, and differences-in-differences. To that end, students will learn about regressions (OLS), how they can be understood as extending a mean comparison t-test, and why it is a frequently used statistical method in economic research. Lastly, students’ practical skills will be enhanced during the tutorials, during which they will practice using statistical software and analysing data. In period 6, couples of students will write a paper on a pre-selected topic, including their findings, analyses and conclusions. The tutorials during this period will guide them through this process.
description.objectives: After successful completion of the course, students are able to work with Microsoft Excel, give a presentation and feedback, and conduct their own empirical research. This entails being able to:work with formulas, tables, and graphs in Excel;write and give a good pitch;give feedback;describe and apply the methodological concepts of empirical design, replicability, validity, inference, ethics;analyze data with simple OLS regression using statistical software;interpret regression results in relation to (pre-selected) literature used during the course;report the results in an academic paper according to APA standards;use AI in a responsible manner for the assignment.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: Organisational EconomicsIn this part of the course, the main question we will tackle is how organisations can optimally incentivise their employees. Students will get acquainted with a range of different contracts and incentive schemes, and we will discuss their advantages and disadvantages from both theoretical and empirical and behavioural points of view. The aim is for students to learn to recognise situations in which a particular model may apply.The following topics are covered:individual performance pay and team incentives;comparative performance evaluation and tournaments;perverse incentives;how companies can find the right employees and how employees can signal their quality to companies in the presence of asymmetric information.Industrial organisationThis part of the course is built around the concept of market power (the ability of a company to charge a price above marginal cost). Students will learn why most companies have some degree of market power and how companies can actively acquire market power. Furthermore, students will learn to analyse the likelihood of collusion in a given market. We will discuss real-world examples of cartels and tacit collusion and how companies can actively facilitate collusion.The following topics are covered:measuring market power and market concentration;understanding and solving models of strategic interaction between companies in an oligopolistic setting;how the government can regulate monopolies and prevent the emergence of market power;price discrimination;auctions and market design.Game TheoryThe course covers the basics of game theory to the extent necessary to tackle the topics mentioned above. The following topics are covered:solving simultaneous games using the Nash equilibrium;solving dynamic games using backward induction;infinitely repeated games, trigger strategies and discounting;asymmetric information.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:solve simple game-theoretic models;recognise and apply the basic concepts and principles of industrial organisation;recognise and apply the basic concepts and principles of organisational economics;analyse and evaluate the strategic choices of companies;analyse and evaluate the organisational structures of companies;recognise and apply the basic principles of European competition law.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, Minor Microeconomics: Markets and Organizations or Minor Economics: Transition Minor.

description.contents: Financial markets play a critical role in our economy. In this course, we introduce the students to the field of finance. Subsequent finance courses in the second and third years will build on the insights developed in this course. Thereto, we will acquaint the students with some basic principles in finance, such as the law of one price applied to financial markets, the time value of money, discounting and compounding, the concept of market value versus book value, basic capital budgeting and valuation techniques (internal rate of return and net present value), the concept of market efficiency, modern portfolio theory and the capital asset pricing model (CAPM). Finally, students will learn about working capital management: how to measure the financing needs, how to manage cash and accounts receivable and accounts payable positions and finally, how to manage inventories.
description.objectives: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to:apply the principles of ‘no arbitrage’ and ‘the law of one price’ in the valuation of securities;discount (compound), a stream of cash flows against the appropriate discount (compound) rate;use the internal rate of return and the net present value in capital budgeting while being aware of their pitfalls;calculate the value of bonds and stocks and use the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) to determine the expected rate of return of security;calculate expected returns, the standard deviation of returns, and create optimal portfolios using expected returns and standard deviations on the basis of Modern Portfolio Theory;establish the financing needs of a corporation on the basis of pro-forma financial statements and understand the trade-offs in working capital management.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Fiscale Economie.

description.contents: The course offers a thorough introduction to the theory and practice of banking as well as monetary economics and monetary policy. The main topics are:the concept of real and nominal rates, bonds and returns;the theoretical determinants of interest rates;main theories on the risk and term structure of interest rates;concepts and theoretical insights on financial structure, the way financial institutions operate as well as the regulation of the financial system;theoretical models on the money supply process and the structure, objectives and policies of central banks;theoretical insights into the causes of financial crises;applications of the concepts and theoretical models: the relevance of the term structure of interest rates to financial planning and monetary policy; current developments in banking and regulation; the impact of monetary policy decisions of central banks, including unconventional policy measures such as quantitative easing;a thorough analysis of the sub-prime financial crisis of 2007-2008 with a focus on the dynamics and the lessons that can be drawn from this crisis;evaluation of the (potential) extension of the mandate of central banks towards the fight against climate change.The course Money and Banking builds upon the concepts introduced in the entry courses. The course content provides students with the required theoretical and conceptual background to participate successfully in the subsequent courses International Money and Finance, Macroeconomics 2, and Monetary and Fiscal Policy.
description.objectives: After successful completion of the course, students:can define and describe the main theoretical concepts as well as practical dimensions of the economics of banking and the workings of the financial system. Students can also explain the theory behind and the practice of formulating monetary policy by central banks, as exemplified by the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve;can apply the concepts and theoretical models to actual developments regarding the financial system and monetary policy;can report in a well-structured manner on current developments of the financial system, financial crises, banking regulation and monetary policies;can critically evaluate various developments in the field of banking, monetary economics and monetary policy, such as the current objectives of and dangers to monetary policy, developments in banking and regulation, as well as the causes of and responses to financial crises such as the subprime financial crisis of 2007-2008;can evaluate the (potential) extension of the mandate of central banks towards the fight against climate change.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Macroeconomics 1, Macroeconomics for Quantitative Economics, Principles of Economics , Economics for a Changing World II.

description.contents: the theory will be discussed during twelve lectures, illustrated by many examples;based on the notes, the syllabus, and the textbook, students will be asked to prepare a collection of exercises before each weekly tutorial. These exercises test proper understanding and application of all relevant concepts;during the tutorials, the exercises are discussed in detail with particular attention to choosing the proper analysis method;additional exercises that will be studied in class can be made available during the tutorials.
description.objectives: At the end of this course, students will be able to:correctly perform techniques from the theory of estimation and hypothesis testing when comparing two populations in independent and matched pairs situations;choose - given a specific research question - the correct statistical technique of analysis in the above situations;perform chi-squared tests (variance, goodness-of-fit, and contingency tables);understand basic theory in simple linear regression: to calculate estimates of the coefficients in simple linear regression models, to correctly perform tests about the coefficients, to predict the value of the dependent variable (with its limitations) and to include categorical variables as independent variables;check for the necessary requirements when using linear regression (regression diagnostics);correctly interpret SPSS and STATA output of the statistical analyses in situations as mentioned above, both for drawing conclusions and for diagnostic purposes;appreciate a research-oriented attitude, a quantitative and analytical approach to problems in economic practice.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Statistics 1 for Economics or Statistics and Probability: especially hypothesis testing for one population.

description.contents: This course focuses on regression analysis, which is a powerful tool to analyse empirical relationships in applied economics. Firstly, the linear regression model will be discussed, including its estimation with ordinary least squares (OLS) and testing hypotheses with t- and F-tests. Particular attention will be paid to the statistical assumptions underlying the basic model. These assumptions should be valid in applications in order to give reliable results. Secondly, this course covers various specification issues: multicollinearity, functional form and qualitative variables. Third, the consequences of deviations from the statistical assumptions underlying OLS (and t- and F-tests) will be examined. We will focus on heteroskedasticity, omitted variable bias, measurement error and simultaneity bias and their effects on estimation and hypothesis testing. The students will learn how to detect possible misspecification with formal statistical tests and how to adapt statistical inference methods in order to get reliable estimation and testing outcomes. An alternative estimation technique, Maximum Likelihood, the probit and logit models in particular, will be discussed as well. In the computer classes, the estimation techniques and testing procedures are applied to artificial and real-world economic data.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:explain the theoretical background of the linear regression, logit and probit models;apply linear regression, logit and probit models to real data and interpret the estimation results;test relevant hypotheses using t- and F-tests;assess whether the basic assumptions of the linear regression model hold, explain what the problems are if these assumptions are violated and find proper solutions for any form of misspecification (heteroskedasticity, nonlinearities, endogeneity);apply alternative estimation techniques (in particular IV and 2SLS) to get consistent estimation results.
description.entryRequirements: Enrollment in B Economics and Business Economics or Minor Economics: Transition Minor.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Students are strongly advised to rehearse Mathematics 1 for Economics, Statistics 1 for Economics, Statistics 2 for Economics and Research Project. Chapters 2 and 3 of Stock and Watson (2020) list the statistical subjects students are required to understand.Moreover, students are expected to have a strong quantitative and analytical background. In particular, students should be familiar with the concepts of differential calculus, exponential and logarithmic functions, second-order derivatives and partial derivatives, chain rule, product rule and quotient rule, summation and product of many variables, random variable, probability distribution, probability density function (PDF), cumulative distribution function (CDF), expectation, variance and correlation. Furthermore, students should know the concepts of estimation and hypothesis testing, p-values and confidence intervals.

description.contents: In international economics, academics typically distinguish between the real/production and monetary/financial sides. This course focuses on the latter in theory, practice, and policy (the course International Trade and Investment covers the real/production side).The following topics will be addressed:main concepts on the foreign exchange market, such as spot and forward markets, hedging and central-bank interventions;concepts such as the balance of payments, international capital flows and international sources of risk;theoretical models on the balance of payments, the exchange rate and their interdependencies;theoretical insights regarding arbitrage and speculation in financial markets, the effects of macroeconomic policy in open economies, the international consequences of economic policy decisions, the optimal exchange rate system for countries, the tensions between domestic and international policy goals and the added value of international cooperation;the history and current situation of the international monetary system, including monetary cooperation via the International Monetary Fund, currency crises and debt crises in emerging market economies, EMU, and the euro.This course builds upon the concepts introduced in the introductory courses. It prepares students to participate successfully in subsequent courses, particularly in Finance, International Economics, and Macroeconomics.
description.objectives: After successful completion of the course, students will be able to:define and describe the main concepts, theoretical models and practical dimensions in the field of international monetary relations and international finance, such as the drivers and effects of international capital flows, the working and dynamics of foreign exchange markets and the international consequences of national economic policy decisions;critically evaluate various historical as well as actual developments in this field, such as the size of current-account imbalances and balance of payments crises;report on economic mechanisms in this field in a structured and precise manner.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Business Administration, B Business Analytics, Minor Economics: Transition Minor, Minor Macroeconomics: International and Monetary Economics, Exchange Exchange Programme UvA Economics and Business, B Bèta-gamma

description.contents: What is economic science? The answer to this question is implicit in the different assumptions, techniques and methods of argumentation used by economists. This course examines and analyses these different assumptions, techniques and methods of argumentation. It addresses the following subjects:diversity of views about the nature of economics as a science and its consequences;sociological aspects of economics and the academic community;methods of economic research and their problems (evidence, induction, deduction and testing);types of assumptions and their consequences;types of economic models and their relation to economic reality;types of explanation and their methodological framework;criteria for appraising the results of research.These subjects will be investigated in themselves as well as in relation to the various fields of economics research.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students:can explain current philosophical justifications of and approaches towards knowledge and methodology in economics;can explain how the diverse aims of economics as a science require diverse forms of methodological appraisal;can defend existing positions about the status of economics as a science.
description.entryRequirements: B Economics and Business Economics, B Actuarial Science, B Business Analytics, B Business Administration, B Econometrics and Data Science and Exchange Exchange Programme UvA Economics and Business.

description.contents: Part 1Optimisation techniques in a setting with constraints. Extensions of the theory presented in the course Mathematics 1 for Economics. Connection between the primal and the dual problem, (in)direct utility functions, (quasi)-concave functions, compensated and uncompensated demand functions, Slutsky relations, the elasticity of substitution, production functions and homothetic functions. Homogeneous functions and Euler's theorem. Short-run and Long-run Total Cost functions.Part 2The theory of Linear Algebra that is needed for the analysis of discrete and continuous dynamic systems. Matrix Calculus. Linear difference/differential equations of the first and second order. Systems of linear difference equations. Parameter analysis and Stability of equilibria in dynamic models. Application of the theory in micro- and macro-economic models.Part 3Solving dynamic models using the software package Matlab.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:apply static optimisation techniques - especially the method of Lagrange - to microeconomic optimisation problems and give an economic interpretation of the results;perform elementary matrix operations;use matrix calculus to describe dynamic economic processes;solve first and second-order linear difference equations and differential equations and interpret the results;calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices and use these to analyse dynamic economic models (systems of linear difference equations and linear differential equations);analyse the convergence/divergence of linear dynamic systems.
description.entryRequirements: Mathematics 1 for Economics or Mathematics and enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, BSc Politics, Psychology, Law and Economics, Exchange Exchange Programme UvA Economics and Business, BSc Bèta-Gamma, Minor Economics: Transition Minor, Pre-master Economics and Business Economics.

description.contents: This course builds up to the theory of general equilibrium in competitive markets, covering preferences and utility, demand theory, choice under uncertainty, production and supply theory and partial competitive equilibrium. Central to the question is how value is determined and shared in a competitive economy. We study how consumer and producer behaviour can be analysed formally, how market outcomes can be derived under various conditions, and the welfare properties of such outcomes. While the first-year course surveyed some of the basic concepts, here, the focus is on a thorough quantitative analysis of the foundations of microeconomic theory. Solving analytical problems, focusing on constrained and unconstrained optimisations, is a central part of this course. The value of concepts such as the utility function, risk aversion, expected utility, contingent demand for inputs, short and long-run supply, consumer and producer surplus, Pareto efficiency and the contract curve will be made clear with illustrations from everyday life. Time will be devoted to understanding measures of welfare (what they mean, their properties and limitations). The real-world and policy relevance of these tools and concepts is stressed throughout the course, with continuous references to current events and debates.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:obtain a deep knowledge of the formal foundations of the basic microeconomic models of consumer behaviour, producer behaviour, and the functioning of markets in partial and general equilibrium models, including models with uncertainty;understand the elementary structure of general equilibrium theory;obtain the skills to solve microeconomic models;formulate the essence of specific economic issues in formal models so they can be analyzed rigorously.
description.entryRequirements: Microeconomics 1 or Microeconomics for AE or Principles of Economics and enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics, B Actuarial Science, B Econometrics and Data Science, B Business Analytics, BSc Bèta-Gamma, BSc Politics, Psychology, Law and Economics, Exchange Exchange Programme UvA Economics and Business, Minor Economics: Transition Minor, Minor Microeconomics: Markets and Organizations, Pre-master Economics and Business Economics.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: A solid foundation in Mathematics (Algebra, Analysis) and Economic Principles (or Microeconomics I).

description.contents: This is a course in empirical research for identifying causal relationships. During the course, students are exposed to different research designs that are commonly used by economists and other social scientists, including standard regression techniques, randomised field experiments, instrumental variable strategies, regression discontinuity designs, fixed-effects regression models, and difference-in-differences approaches. The emphasis is on understanding the techniques involved and on what they mean in terms of the economic problem being studied. For each method, students learn statistical and econometric techniques, read empirical applications in micro- and macroeconomics, and work with data by applying the method in STATA.
description.objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:go through multiple stages of empirical research (recognising/finding relevant economic research questions, devising an appropriate causal research design, processing data, and implementing the econometric analysis);understand empirical strategies to conduct causal inference (including standard regression techniques, randomised field experiments, instrumental variable strategies, regression discontinuity designs, fixed-effects regression models, and difference-in-differences approaches).
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: Research Project, Statistics 1 for Economics, Statistics 2 for Economics, Econometrics.

description.contents: Game theory is about strategically interdependent decision-making. In such situations, the result of a decision depends on the decisions of others. When making a decision, people have to think about what others will do, who are thinking about what others do, and so on. Game theory offers several concepts and insights for understanding and analysing such situations and for making better strategic decisions. This course will teach how a game that corresponds to an economic situation should be formulated. It introduces the most important equilibrium concepts that are needed to analyse strategic interaction and illustrates these concepts with some applications. This course is analytically challenging and requires a willingness and ability to think.Equilibrium concepts:Nash equilibrium;Subgame perfect equilibrium;Bayesian Nash equilibrium;(weak) Sequential equilibrium.Applications:oligopoly;auctions;public goods;bargaining;adverse selection;signalling;electoral competition and voting.The materials studied in this course provide students with the required theoretical and conceptual background that will allow them to participate successfully in the subsequent courses Behavioural Economics, Public Economics, Organisational Economics and Industrial Organisation.
description.objectives: Upon completing this course, students:are able to formulate a game that corresponds to an economic situation;understand which equilibrium concept is appropriate to analyse the game;are able to analyse the game and derive the game-theoretic predictions;are able to think critically about the predictions and, if necessary, improve the game description and analysis.
description.entryRequirements: B Business Analytics, B Fiscal Economics, B Economics and Business Economics (Major Economics), Minor Economics: Transition Minor, Minor Microeconomics: Markets and Organizations, Pre-master Economics and Business Economics and Exchange Exchange Programme UvA Economics and Business.
description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: This is a challenging course. A willingness and ability to think analytically are necessary.

description.contents: Macroeconomics studies economic behaviour at the aggregate level, trying to explain phenomena such as economic growth, unemployment, and inflation. It also deals with the design of policies (in particular, monetary and fiscal policy) that may improve the functioning of the economy. In this course, the following topics will be discussed:essential concepts in macroeconomics, such as structural and cyclical unemployment, public deficits, and debts;different theories of consumption and investment behaviour, their empirical performance, and their implications for economic policy;theoretical insights on the time-inconsistency of monetary policies;the theory of economic growth according to the Solow model, its implications for the convergence between countries, and the decomposition of economic growth;the critical discussion of current developments in the field of macroeconomics, such as convergence in economic growth, the design of monetary and fiscal policies, and the controversies on the sustainability of public deficits.This course builds upon the concepts introduced during the entry courses and considerably expands the depth and breadth of their topics. It offers the knowledge required for the course Macroeconomics in the M Economics.
description.objectives: After successful completion of the course, students:can define the main concepts of Macroeconomics at a level beyond the course Macroeconomics 1;can describe the main theories of macroeconomics and their empirical evidence and policy implications;can reflect on the advantages and disadvantages of macroeconomic policy (mainly fiscal and monetary);can reproduce knowledge about current developments and controversies in macroeconomics;can collect relevant data, use underlying algebra, and discuss various crucial concepts in the field of macroeconomics [within the take-home assignments].
description.entryRequirements: Macroeconomics 1 or Macroeconomics for Quantitative Economics or Principles of Economics and enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics or B Actuarial Science or B Econometrics and Data Science or B Fiscale Economie or Exchange Exchange Programme UvA Economics and Business or BSc Bèta-Gamma or Minor Economics: Transition Minor or Minor Macroeconomics: International and Monetary Economics or Pre-master Economics and Business Economics.

description.contents: Why are some countries poor and other countries rich? How do people cope with being poor in an uncertain, sometimes hostile environment? What sort of policies work in the fight against poverty? Can countries really accelerate economic growth through better-designed policies? What do both economic growth theories and empirical research suggest with respect to the determinants of growth? What are the historical trends in economic growth across regions? What is the relationship between health and economic growth? What is the relation between population growth and economic growth?In this course, we try to answer these questions from both an international economics and macroeconomics growth theory perspective as well as from a micro perspective. The macro perspective segment will focus on the drivers of growth, and we will use Ray (1998) to discuss several growth theories, trends in economic growth, inequality and poverty, measurement issues with respect to economic growth (chapters 1 to 4) and the relation between population growth and economic growth (chapter 9). In the micro perspective segment, we will draw on Schaffner (2013) and articles to investigate the role of geography and institutions. We will discuss different approaches to impact evaluation and apply these to investigate the impact of tropical diseases and anti-poverty programs.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students will have learned to:explain differences in growth and poverty using the main theories in development economics;apply these theories to economic problems facing developing countries;discuss topics from development economics in a broad perspective using results from the empirical literature;indicate the relevance of theories and empirical results for development policies;write an essay on a topic in development economics that coherently reviews the literature and adds some empirical work.

description.recommendedPriorKnowledge: We will assume a basic knowledge of statistics (compare means), regression analysis (OLS), game theory (Nash equilibrium) and consumer demand (utility function).

description.contents: Introduction to Python aims to provide students with an understanding of and some experience in writing scripts (programs).Python is a multi-purpose programming language that is relatively easy for students to learn and is used in several economic fields, inside and outside academia. While it is not possible to cover all the aspects of a computer language in six weeks, after this course, students should be able to operate independently using mainly online resources. Students will design, write, and run Python scripts in a development environment.In the first two weeks, the focus is on learning the basics of the Python language. During tutorials and at home, students will have to write little programs. In the last four weeks, the focus will be on expanding their knowledge of Python.Besides standard plenary lectures (regular lectures and feedback lectures), there will be guest lectures by Python professionals in fields like finance, big data, machine learning, and experimental economics to give students an idea about the usefulness of Python in their future careers.
description.objectives: Upon completion of this course, students are able:to set up and use a development environment for designing and writing Python scripts;to understand the basics of Python: datatypes, conditional statements and loops, functions, objects, and classes;to translate the solutions of simple problems into Python scripts;to forecast the result of a Python script;to compare different solutions to simple programming problems.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Business Administration, B Economics and Business Economics or B Fiscal Economics.

description.contents: The course discusses the emergence of the main strands in economics on the basis of the theories of their founders. Starting with Smith and Ricardo, we move to Marx, and next via Jevons and Marshall to Keynes and Friedman. Subsequently, we discuss the historical background of the current orthodoxy in economics. We will see that the research techniques of economists have changed over time. This change is connected with changing conceptual frameworks. These again are in part related to specific historical contexts as well as in part to views on economic relations and entities (e.g. 'money is merely a veil' or 'money is key to the functioning of market economies'; or 'individual behaviour is determined by macro relations' versus 'macro relations are best understood as aggregated individual behaviour'). In the tutorials, students are challenged to apply these alternative visions to contemporary problems and argue how they can still be considered relevant (or not).
description.objectives: After completion of the course, students will be able to:present an overview of the main authors and strands within the history of economics from 1775 till at least 2000;appreciate past theories and ideas in their historical context;evaluate the relevance of these historical perspectives for understanding the causes of and finding potential solutions for contemporary problems in the economy.

description.contents: The course starts with an overview of the standard static and dynamic models of quantity and price competition in oligopolistic markets. In the second week, we study anti-competitive practices, such as entry deterrence and predation, followed by a week on cartel agreements. In the second half of the course, we apply the basic models of the first week to study mergers, vertical market structure, and the strategic role of research and development.The level of the discussion will be intermediate: deep enough to convey the main insights of the models in a technical manner while ignoring many of the finer details. The tutorials and homework assignments will provide many opportunities for practice on numerical problems.
description.objectives: The aim of the course is to provide students with an economic framework for analysing imperfectly competitive markets and to connect the theory to real-life strategic behaviour through short case studies and econometric analyses.Upon completing the course, students will be able to:model competition between large firms with strategic motivations;distinguish predatory behaviour from regular competitive actions;analyse motivations for collusive behaviour and predict the stability of cartels;analyse motivations for mergers and how they impact welfare;discuss how vertical price and non-price restraints can be used to overcome the double marginalisation problem;discuss what the models imply for corporate strategy and public policy in the real world.

uva-ebe-y3-thesis.name: Bachelor's Thesis and Thesis Seminar Economics

description.contents: The Thesis Seminar offers students general guidance in writing the bachelor's thesis. Students are guided through the process of writing a thesis. The individual supervision is in the hands of the thesis supervisor. The thesis supervisor will be assigned during the course.The Bachelor's Thesis: objectivesA Bachelor's Thesis is an academic paper in which a research question is developed and answered through a literature review, supplemented with original empirical and/or theoretical research. This implies that a thesis has the following components:a research question with a thorough motivation as to why this question is interesting to investigate further;an overview of the relevant theories which are used in the literature related to the research question;a detailed discussion of the relevant empirical literature related to the research question;a synthesis where you answer the research question based on the available theoretical and empirical literature;a theoretical and/or empirical part that builds on the second and third items from this list to support your synthesis.As a guideline, a bachelor's thesis should contain 5,000 to 9,000 words. However, deviations from this are possible, although it is unlikely that a thesis containing less than 5,000 words meets the criteria for a passing grade.AI use is allowed provided the student adheres to the rules specific to the thesis.
description.objectives: The aim for this course is to provide general guidance in writing a Bachelor’s thesis. During the course, students must demonstrate their ability to:conduct research of at least bachelor-level quality and report and present work in progress;handle feedback effectively and constructively;work in a professional and ethical manner.
description.entryRequirements: Enrolment in B Economics and Business Economics.At least 90 EC must be completed before the start of the academic year in which the course is taken, and 120 EC must be completed at the start of the course.A place in this course is only guaranteed for students who have registered their specialisation before 1 October 2026 and register for the course during the course registration period starting on 30 November 2026.

progression: The first year comprises ten compulsory 6 EC units in two 30 EC semesters, with the Research Project in the second semester. Passing all 60 EC supplies the quantitative, economics and research background for year two.

Five common courses in the first semester total 30 EC. The five named Economics requirements in the second semester total 30 EC. Research Laboratory recommends the year-one project, Statistics 1 and 2 and Econometrics. Game Theory precedes the selected third-year Development Economics course; Economics of Markets and Organisations satisfies Industrial Organisation entry.

The first semester of year three preserves 30 EC of approved choice. The catalogue requires 24 EC restricted electives and a 6 EC thesis and seminar. Select Development Economics and Introduction to Python in period 4 and History of Economic Thought and Industrial Organisation in period 5 by published order among options in those periods. These leave room for the semester-long thesis. The thesis requires 90 EC before the academic year and 120 EC at the start of the course. The completed first two years satisfy both thresholds; timely registration is required.
